question: What version of Saul's death does the Amalekite tell David, and what does he bring as proof?
Why does David condemn the Amalekite, and how does this connect with what he himself did in 1 Samuel 24 and 26?
The lament repeats “How the mighty have fallen,” with גִּבּוֹר (gibbor, “mighty man, hero”): what image of Saul and Jonathan does the poem preserve, and what does it leave aside?
David mourns both the king who pursued him and his friend: how do you deal with grief for someone with whom the relationship was complicated?
What does David ask the LORD before moving, and what happens in Hebron?
The verb עָלָה (‘alah, “go up”) appears in David's inquiry and his move to Hebron: what contrast is there between this guided going up and the way Ish-bosheth is put on the throne?
What does the “contest” of twelve against twelve by the pool of Gibeon reveal about the conflict between the houses of Saul and David?
Abner asks “Must the sword devour forever?”: what conflict in your life would need someone with the courage to ask this question?
Why does Abner break with Ish-bosheth, and what does he promise to do?
The word בַּיִת (bayit, “house”) appears in the sense of family and dynasty throughout the chapter: what “houses” are in dispute, and what happens to each one?
What motives does the text attribute to Joab in killing Abner, and how does this threaten the plan to unite Israel?
Why is David's public mourning for Abner important for the people, according to the text itself?
David admits being a king still “weak” before hard men at his side: in what situation do you feel you do not control those who act in your name?
How do Rechab and Baanah kill Ish-bosheth, and what do they hope to gain by bringing his head to David?
Why does the narrator interrupt the story to introduce Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son?
Ish-bosheth's רֹאשׁ (rosh, “head”) is brought as a trophy and then buried beside Abner: what does this contrast say about how David wants the kingdom to come to him?
The murderers think they are pleasing David: when has someone tried to “help” you in a way you could not approve?
What three reasons do the tribes give for making David king over all Israel?
The verb מָשַׁח (mashach, “anoint”) appears when Israel anoints David and when the Philistines hear the news: what does this anointing by the people add to Samuel's in 1 Samuel 16?
What changes between the two battles against the Philistines in the Valley of Rephaim, and what does this show about the way David decides?
David understands that he was exalted “for the sake of His people Israel”: whom should the place or influence you have serve?
How is the ark carried from the house of Abinadab, and what happens at the threshing floor of Nacon?
Why does Uzzah's death frighten David, and what do the three months in the house of Obed-edom show by contrast?
The verb בָרַךְ (barakh, “bless”) passes through Obed-edom, the people and David's house: how does this chain of blessing end in the encounter with Michal?
David accepts looking “undignified” to celebrate before God: what weighs more for you when expressing your faith, sincerity or the opinion of others?
What does David propose to Nathan, and what is the LORD's first response to this idea?
How does the promise play on the two senses of “house,” building and descendants, and what is promised to David's line?
The word עוֹלָם (‘olam, “forever”) is repeated in the promise and the prayer: how have Jews and Christians, each in their own way, read this “forever” throughout history?
David asks “Who am I, and what is my house?”: when have you received something that seemed too great for you, and how did you react?
Against which peoples does David fight in this chapter, and what does he do with the gold, silver and bronze he receives?

The verb נָכָה (nakah, “strike, defeat”) opens almost every paragraph of the account: how should we read today a list of victories so marked by violence, including the treatment of the Moabites in verse 2?
The refrain “the LORD gave David victory” is followed by the sentence about “justice and righteousness”: what relationship does the text suggest between David's success and the way he governs?
David “administered justice and righteousness for all his people”: in what space under your responsibility can you practice justice concretely?
What question does David ask about the house of Saul, and who gives him the information about Mephibosheth?
The word חֵסֵד (chesed, “kindness, covenant loyalty”) appears three times: to what promise made in the past is David being faithful here?
What change of situation does the text show between Mephibosheth calling himself a “dead dog” and the end of the chapter, which places him at the king's table?
David actively looks for someone to show kindness to: is there someone in your life you could seek out because of an old friendship or promise?
What intention does David have in sending his servants to Hanun, and how are they treated?
What role does the suspicion of the Ammonite princes play in the war that follows?
The verb חָזַק (chazaq, “be strong”) appears in the agreement between Joab and Abishai: how does their courage combine with “may the LORD do what is good in His sight”?
David protects the dignity of the humiliated servants by having them wait in Jericho: how can you care for someone who has gone through public shame?
Where is David “in the spring, at the time when kings march out to war,” and what sequence of actions leads him to Bathsheba?
The verb שָׁלַח (shalach, “send”) appears from beginning to end of the chapter: what does this repetition reveal about how David uses power?
What contrast does the text draw between the conduct of Uriah, a foreign Hittite, and that of the king of Israel?
The chapter ends with the LORD's judgment after a long silence: what attitudes of yours have you perhaps tried to “resolve” by hiding instead of facing?
How does Nathan tell the story of the rich man and the poor man, and what sentence does David pronounce before knowing whom it concerns?
Why does Nathan choose a parable instead of a direct accusation, and what does it make David see?
The verb צוּם (tsum, “fast”) appears while the child lives and is abandoned after his death: how does David explain this change to his servants?
David answers Nathan with “I have sinned against the LORD,” without excuses: what makes it hard for you to acknowledge a mistake so directly?
What role does Jonadab play in Amnon's plan, and how does David end up involved without knowing it?
What does Tamar say to try to stop Amnon, and why does she consider being sent away an even greater wrong?
The verb חָלָה (chalah, “be sick”) describes first Amnon's anguish and then his feigned illness: what does this passage from feeling to pretense reveal about him?
How do David and Absalom react to what happened to Tamar, and what is left undone?
Tamar is told to keep quiet and remains “desolate”: how can you and your community listen to and protect those who have suffered abuse, instead of asking for silence?
What story does the woman of Tekoa tell the king, and what promise does she manage to draw from him?
What does the woman mean by the image of “water spilled on the ground” and by the idea that God devises ways so that the banished one is not cast out?
The word פָּנִים (panim, “face”) marks Absalom's incomplete return, as he does not see the king's face: what do this delayed reunion and then the final kiss leave open?
David brings Absalom back but does not receive him: is there someone with whom you have “made peace” only halfway?
What does Absalom do every morning by the gate, and how does he treat those who come with a lawsuit?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice, case”) is at the center of Absalom's strategy: how does he use the kingdom's lack of justice to “steal the hearts” of Israel?
Why does David try to send Ittai back, and what does this foreigner's answer show about loyalty?
What does the decision to send the ark back to Jerusalem reveal about how David understands his relationship with God in this crisis?
David goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, but still prays and acts: how do you combine surrender and initiative when everything seems to be falling apart?
What does Ziba bring to David, and what does he say about Mephibosheth?
The verb קָלַל (qalal, “curse”) is repeated in the scene with Shimei: why does David stop Abishai from reacting, and what does he hope from God in the face of these curses?
How does Ahithophel's advice fulfill what Nathan had announced in 2 Samuel 12:11-12?
David lets Shimei speak and says “perhaps the LORD will see my affliction”: what unfair, or partly fair, criticism do you need to learn to hear without striking back?
What plans do Ahithophel and Hushai propose to Absalom, and how do they differ?
The word עֵצָה (‘etsah, “counsel”) is at the center of the chapter: what does verse 14 reveal about who is acting behind human decisions?
What does Ahithophel's end reveal about the weight he gave to his own counsel and his reputation?
People from different places, even an Ammonite, bring food to David in the wilderness: who has shown up with practical help at a moment when you were exhausted?
How does David organize the army, why do the people not let him go out, and what order does he give about Absalom?
Why does the soldier refuse to kill Absalom, and what does Joab's attitude show about him?
The verb בָּשַׂר (basar, “bring good news”) appears in the race of Ahimaaz and the Cushite: why is a military victory not good news for David?
David's lament repeats “my son” several times: what pain of yours is still tied to words unsaid or to a relationship left unmended?
How does the victory turn into mourning for the people, and what does Joab demand of David?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return, bring back”) dominates the discussion about bringing the king back: who takes the initiative for this return, and what tensions between the tribes does it reveal?
How does David treat Shimei, Mephibosheth and Ziba on the way back, and what do his decisions suggest about the king at this moment?
Barzillai refuses the reward and asks to die in his own city: what does his attitude teach about knowing one's own measure and time?
What cry does Sheba raise, and what is the reaction of the men of Israel and of Judah?
How does Joab get rid of Amasa, and why does the narrator describe the body on the road in such detail?
The wise woman calls Abel “a city that is a mother in Israel,” using עִיר (‘ir, “city”): how does she manage to save the city without a battle?
The woman of Abel asks an armed general to “listen to the words of your servant”: in what conflict could you be the voice that proposes a way out other than force?
What cause does the LORD point to for the three-year famine, and what do the Gibeonites ask of David?
The handing over of Saul's seven descendants is one of the most disturbing episodes of the book: what logic of oath and guilt does the text assume, and how do you deal with it today?
The word עֶצֶם (‘etsem, “bones”) is repeated when David gathers the remains of Saul, Jonathan and those who were hanged: why does this burial seem to end the crisis in the land?
Rizpah watches over her sons' bodies for weeks, until the king notices her grief: what silent pain around you is waiting to be noticed?
What happens to David in the battle against Ishbi-benob, and why do his men decide he will no longer go out to war?
With what images does David describe the danger he was delivered from, and what did he do at that moment?
What do the images of earthquake, fire, clouds and thunder communicate about the way God comes to David's rescue?
The adjective תָּמִים (tamim, “blameless, perfect”) is used for David and for God's way: how should we understand David calling himself blameless after all the book has narrated?
“The LORD lights my darkness”: what dark area of your life would you like to see lit up?
How does David present himself in his last words, and with what images does he describe the just ruler?
Why does David pour out on the ground the water the three mighty men risked their lives to bring?
The word שֵׁם (shem, “name”) appears in the list of mighty men who “won a name”: what does it mean that the chapter ends with the name of Uriah the Hittite?
David perceives the human cost of a wish of his and changes his attitude: what desire of yours weighs on other people without your noticing?
What does David order to be done, who tries to dissuade him, and how long does the task take?
This chapter says the LORD incited David, while 1 Chronicles 21:1 speaks of an adversary: how have readers of different traditions understood this difference?
The verb קָנָה (qanah, “buy”) appears when David insists on paying for Araunah's threshing floor: why does he refuse to receive the place for free?
David asks that the punishment fall on him and not on “these sheep”: in what situation do you need to take on the consequences of a mistake instead of letting them fall on others?
